utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Tuesday, the 14th of July, 2009. I would like to welcome Mr. Praljak, first of all, Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Pusic. I would also like to welcome Mr. Coric. We've had good news from him. I would also like to greet Defence counsel, Mr. Stringer and his entire team, without forgetting all the staff members assisting us. I have, first of all, an administrative piece of information to disclose to you. Pursuant to a video conference which will take place tomorrow afternoon in another case, we have been asked to sit in the morning tomorrow. Tomorrow morning, we will sit at 9.00, and according to the Registrar's chart we will be in Courtroom I. I also have an oral decision to hand down, which I shall do now, and I shall read it out slowly. Oral decision concerning the disclosure of documents by the Prosecution as part of its cross-examination of the Accused Praljak. At the hearing of the 13th of July, 2009, Praljak's Defence asked the Prosecution to disclose to the Defence teams those documents it intends to use for its cross-examination of the accused Praljak, and this should be done with sufficient advance notice to enable them to study these documents. The Prosecution responded by saying that it intended to conduct its cross-examination on the basis of various topics. And since the Trial Chamber had authorised it to do so, it would disclose the documents it intends to use in batches, and would do so as soon as possible. In light of the parties' comments, and with a view to guaranteeing efficient proceedings, the Trial Chamber is asking the Prosecution, first of all, to provide the Trial Chamber, as well as the Defence teams, a list of topics it intends to deal with during its cross-examination, and this should be done by the 17th of August, 2009, at the latest, as well as all the documents it will submit as part of an individual topic it will deal with from this date onwards. Thereafter, as soon as possible, and before finishing its presentation on one topic, the Prosecution should disclose to the Trial Chamber and the Defence teams those documents it intends to submit as part of the next topic. So, in short, to be clear, Mr. Stringer will disclose to us, by the 17th of August, 2009, at the latest, the list of topics, but if the Prosecution discloses the latter earlier, all the better, as well as a list of all the documents it will submit during the cross-examination relating to the first topic. And before finishing the first topic, it will disclose to the Defence those documents it intends to use for its next topic. Have you understood everything, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. And good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. And before responding, can I wish the president and any of his French staff a happy Bastille Day. As I understand the ruling of the Trial Chamber, we will be essentially acting in somewhat the fashion that we'd been proceeding this week, and I don't see any difficulty in continuing to do that. And in fact by the time we get beyond the summer recess, I'm sure that we'll be able to -- that the documents that relate to a topic will, we'll be able to continue to disclose them in advance of the beginning of the topic. So I don't see any difficulties, Mr. President, and I don't see any difficulties in providing a list of topics by the 17th of August, at the latest. As I understand the ruling, however, the list of topics is not -- we're not required to include in that list of topics on the 17th of August or sooner a listing of each of the exhibits that fall within each of those topics, and so if that is a correct understanding of the Court's ruling, then I don't see any difficulties on the part of the Prosecution. Mr. President, if I can say, there was one other difficulty that I do foresee, though, and it's based on the rescheduling of tomorrow's proceedings. And if perhaps we could go quickly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem. Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In open session, the cross-examination of the accused Praljak resumes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I did request five minutes to deal with a procedural issue. I don't know whether you want me to deal with this at the end or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't been advised first, but you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I'd like to greet the Chamber and everyone in the courtroom. I really will be very brief. Dr. Prlic's Defence, on the 10th of July, 2009, asked the Trial Chamber to have leave for an interlocutory appeal to the decision of the Chamber on the re-examination of evidence, the decision of the 29th of June, 2009. The Prosecution responded to the request on the 13th of July, 2009. In its response, the OTP erroneously interprets and distorts the arguments presented in the request for this appeal to be granted. The Prosecution claims that this submission is not a request for leave to file interlocutory appeal against the decision of the Chamber on re-examining the evidence of the 29th of June, 2009. It claims it's a request for the authorisation to appeal the decision of the Chamber rendered on the 6th of March, 2009. That is the first basic decision on documentary evidence, and for that decision the dead-line for appeal has, naturally, expired. What the Prosecution is, in fact, claiming in its response is, well, they are accusing the Prlic Defence of wanting to bypass the Rules, and I consider that this is a very serious accusation to which it is necessary to respond. Therefore, I request the Chamber allows us to reply to the Prosecution argument, because there are particular circumstances, and in accordance with the jurisprudence of the Court this request is justified. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tomanovic, the Trial Chamber has decided to certify the appeal, so you are permitted to appeal. We shall record our decision tomorrow. There's no need to reply because we have decided to allow you to authorise the decision. Have you understood?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the night, I thought about today's hearing, and I felt, Mr. Praljak, that I should put a question to you. We know, on the basis of the documents provided by the Republic of Croatia, that there was a Croatian Defence Council which comprised 12 members, and you were a part of this council. We saw that this was presided over by Mr. Tudjman and other generals, and sometimes other people, but on the basis of the document, which indicated that these people had been appointed. Though, the question I have is: As far as Herceg-Bosna is concerned, did the same kind of council exist, and did Mr. Boban, for instance, preside over a defence council where Mr. Prlic and the Generals Praljak, Petkovic, and perhaps other people would have been present, or did this defence council never exist, as far as the HVO was concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While I was down there, there was no such counsel. I believe that subsequently certain attempts were made to make or create something to that effect, something of that nature, but I'm not sure. I was never a member of a similar kind of council in the HVO, and I was never present at a meeting of such a council. So as far as I know, up until the 8th of November, no such council was in existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all I wanted to know. Thank you. Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You have the binder still with you that we were working on yesterday that contains documents related to the international -- what the lawyers called the international armed conflict issue. I'm going to ask you to skip that document that you have in front of you and move to P03667. 3667. It should be just the next document in your binder. We're just going to skip one for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Please correct and put in "to allow you to appeal" and not "to authorise the decision." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, this is a document dated the 23rd of July, 1993, so it's just one day before you take command of the HVO Main Staff, and it is a document of the -- well, it's directed to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, as well as to other bodies, and it's signed for Commander Brigadier Ivan Kapular who I believe was a commander of the 5th Guards Brigade of the Republic of Croatia -- Croatian Army; is that correct? Do you know that Brigadier Kapular was the commander of the 5th Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this document -- we talked a little bit yesterday about the southern front, and I said that we would have a chance to come back to that. Well, we're coming back to that now. This document, at the very first sentence of section 1, says, talking about the daily activities and training, and this is, I should say, coming from the Osijek Military District Military Post 3132 Command, saying that: "Since most of the unit is either on leave or carrying out combat tasks at the southern front, daily activities were reduced to maintenance of material, technical equipment," et cetera. And then if you continue on and to section 2 or paragraph 2 of the same document - I'm on page 2 of the English - the report says that: "The latest events at the southern front, that is to say, the casualties that the tactical group of the 5th Guards Brigade has suffered, has had more negative impact on the civilian sector than on the brigade members itself. For example, there was a spontaneous gathering of parents in Nova Gradiska, in front of the municipal building, where they demanded the return of their children and information on their whereabouts. I would like to mention here that everybody in Nova Gradiska knows where the southern front is, so that particularly negative political connotations occurred in connection with that. We shall send you a detailed report on those events, and we request from you instructions on how to politically handle such cases." Now, General, is it correct that the references here to the southern front are references to members of the 5th Guards Brigade who were down fighting together with or as part of HVO units in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the southern front is referred to here, what they have in mind is the fact that the southern front concerned the part of the volunteers who fought in the HVO. That included the volunteers from the 5th Guards Brigade who were voluntarily fighting within the HVO framework.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there's a southern battle-field, it's a real battle-field, and this term doesn't cover that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So the southern front is -- well, let me take you to some of your earlier testimony, where you talked about that, just so that we can flush this out a bit. I'm looking at the transcript from the 11th of May, 2009, in this case, page 39908, and on that day, General, you testified -- you were responding to a question from Judge Antonetti, and I'll read to you what you said. I'm quoting: "A volunteer or volunteers received a piece of paper saying that he could go, and we called it the southern front. So he would go to the southern front, and that is cover for him if he were to be killed or whatever. That's what I know. That's the extent of my knowledge." Do you recall that testimony, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So the "southern front" is the way, in the Croatian Army, that they kept track of who were fighting as part of the HVO; is that what "southern front" means?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The "southern front" means the following. It's a front that had its own commanders, and they were defending Dubrovnik, the south of Croatia, and naturally the Croatian Army was working on this, in this field. But in addition, apart from the fact that there was this regular battle-field for the defence of Croatia, and that concerned the area from Ploce and further down somewhat towards Split as well, in addition to that there was this aspect, so the southern front was a way of having volunteers on paper, they went to fight for the HVO and to defend from the ABiH attack. If someone was killed or wounded, et cetera, this would be covered, because otherwise it wasn't possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So then in this document that we started with today, P03667, the report here is that, in fact, there are parents and civilians who are protesting about the fact that their children and their sons are being sent down to fight as part of the HVO on the southern front; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that there were spontaneous rallies and protests, but I repeat, nobody came to the HVO to fight without being a volunteer. As I've already said several times, and I've shown you in documents, they could possibly refuse an order of that kind without any military consequences. There were a lot of more problems with regard to this particular rally, because immediately prior to these events, that brigade had suffered a lot of casualties in the Zadar front-line and around Maslenica, which all came to a head and resulted in problems with the parents of those men.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And these volunteers, as you call them, from the 5th Guards Brigade, then, when they were fighting as part of the HVO in Herceg-Bosna - we talked about this yesterday - they remained on the payroll of the Ministry of the Defence of the Republic of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they were transferred, they became the HVO. They were under the command of the HVO, and they were paid by the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. I repeat, this applied to all the volunteers, those who joined the BiH Army as well as those who joined the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the next document, General, is P03886.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. General Praljak, let us remain with this document. Yesterday, through the documents we realised that Mr. Tudjman had people who opposed his action. Yesterday's document was very clear in this respect. Now, if we put this document together with the other one, this one dates back to July, and apparently parents are worried because their children are fighting in a territory which may be -- about which they may not feel concerned. Let's take the example of a Croatian family from Zagreb or the surroundings of Zagreb, and this family learns that their son is now a conscript and that he is in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Maybe his parents are going to wonder what their son is doing over there. At your level, did you learn that parents would, as it were, challenge the fact that their sons were being sent there? You say that they were volunteers. It may be that the son was a volunteer, but the parents did not agree, because if you lose a son, I mean, it's always a tragedy. Even if the son was a volunteer, the parents may have been of a different opinion. Were you aware of such challenges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, even before, when there were similar problems with regard to the departure of volunteers to Posavina. At the time I was a member of the IPD. The 5th Guards Brigade, as I've already told you, and I've told you why the 5th Guards Brigade had volunteers, all of these men who are mentioned, Kapular, Leko and others, 90 per cent of their family names were -- indicate that they were either born in Herzegovina, if they were somewhat older, or their parents hailed from there. And when Slavonia was settled after the expulsion of Folksdojcer, they moved from Herzegovina to Slavonia, and that's why there were so many volunteers in the 5th Guards Brigade. There were very few in the 1st or the 4th Guards Brigade which originated from Zagreb or Split, because those men did not hail from the Herzegovina area, either them or their parents. It is true that next to those men who hailed from the area, some other people volunteered who may have been their friends. For example, if one group went, then everybody went as volunteers, and their parents didn't know about that, and of course there were issues raised and questions raised. From day 1, it was well known -- everybody in Croatia knew that no soldier could be issued an order to go to Herzegovina or anywhere else to fight there if they were not volunteers. I've repeated that myself. Susak hammered on that, Stipetic as well. And as far as some discrepancies with Dr. Franjo Tudjman, there were two groups that were in discord with him. The first group claimed that his policy of being tolerant towards Alija Izetbegovic and the international community brought the HVO and Croats in the position of being perceived as losers, they were losers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can we move briefly to private session. I have to ask this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Praljak, it just strikes me as strange that parents of volunteers, and it must be quite a number of them, parents who are Croats and who you have just affirmed, like everyone else, knew that all soldiers that were in Herceg-Bosna fighting were volunteers, that they gathered spontaneously in Nova Gradiska and demand the return of their children and information on their whereabouts. It simply does not make sense, if they are volunteers, because no one sent them. If they demand to know where they are, maybe that makes some sense so that they can tell them to come back. But if you don't send someone, how can you call someone back? Are the parents just stupid, ill-informed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, the 5th Guards Brigade was a professional brigade, a professional brigade, and at the end of the day the brigade commander could be taken to task, or his commander. But that professional brigade could have been sent to any theatre of war anywhere, without any consequences, save for the consequences due to the war. But some parents -- I even had a rebellion staged by the wives, asking for their husbands to return, those who had remained fighting in Zepce. This was normal in Croatia. Everybody meddled with everything. Their children who were receiving a special allowance and were promised ranks, there were some incentives for the volunteers to raise their morale, that's true, and I am sure that they never said that to their parents, or 90 per cent of them didn't, or some of them didn't. It doesn't say here how many people gathered in Gradiska. I can't speculate on that. But I repeat, and I claim, and you will see that Kapular says that in a document, that those were volunteers and they -- there were fewer of them than mentioned in this document. I knew them by name, almost all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have told us a hundred times that they were volunteers. We have no -- we have heard that many times. Who was volunteers and who was not? When I asked you whether these parents were ignorant, you answered by pointing out that the 5th Guards Brigade, that they were professionals. I don't know whether there's a difference between professional and volunteer. I do not see that, necessarily. Are you saying that they did not complain -- that their gathering did not concern young men who had been fighting as, quote, "volunteers" in Herceg-Bosna? Is that your point, "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, Mr. Praljak. We must get a bit forward. Then you have not really asked my -- answered my question. It does -- in my view, it does not make sense, if parents of volunteers protest in front of a municipal building, before authorities, when their children are away on their own will and the parents know that. I do not find it very convincing to say that everyone protests against everything, because that doesn't make much sense, frankly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, if their parents knew. How do you know that the parents did know? Here you can see that the brigade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I know because Mr. Praljak told me so a few minutes ago. Mr. Praljak said here, Everyone knew that they were volunteers. You have said so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I really don't know how this was interpreted, but this is not correct, this is not correct. This brigade, as you can see, was in the theatre of war, and then it was sent on furlough. Most of the men were on furlough, because they didn't have shirts or trousers. They were not at home. A professional guards brigade, unlike a brigade that is mobilised -- in other words, when a brigade is mobilised, when it's not professional, then the man who is putting on a uniform in his house can tell his parents, I have been summoned, and I'll be a volunteer, and I've accepted to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina. This brigade was never at home, these men were not at home. Those were professional soldiers of the Croatian Army who were in Zadar, and they were exhausted, they had problems, and they were on furlough. Most of the unit was on furlough, and that's what it says here. And one part of them, of volunteers, were still discharging their duties, and those who went down there from furlough and are those who signed the professional contract, and they did not inform their parents. They were not allowed to inform their parents where they were, where they were sent. And I'm speaking very slowly, aren't I? They did not, because they had -- they had an obligation not to tell their parents. They signed professional contracts, but not everything was spelled out quite precisely. In the contracts, some things could not be implemented. You know what the problems were. I don't think that a legionnaire informs his parents every time when he's being sent somewhere; for example, Mom and dad, I'm going to Abu Dhabi now. Bye. They volunteered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have been referring on page 14, line 5. I leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, there's a problem, because we, as Judges, are very much outside the Republic of Croatia and it's difficult for us to know how it operated internally. So I stand to be corrected by you, but am I to understand that there were two types of soldiers during these events, those who had been conscripts, enrolled into the army and doing their military service, and there was another category, people who had contracts and had been enrolled in professional units? Is this how it worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a little more complicated still, Your Honours. There were professional brigades, and that's why I'm always imploring with you to read the whole document, because if you take a sentence out of context, you can't arrive at the truth. The 1st Guards Brigade, the 2nd, the 3rd, the 4th, and let's not go any further, the 5th, the 7th, the 9th and so on and so forth, those were professional guards brigades, professional soldiers with contracts. They had their barracks, they slept there, and they were sent to the field pursuant to orders. And there were also the so-called R brigades which could be mobilised, and then they were sent to a theatre of war, and once the assignment was over they returned their uniforms and went back home, and the next unit would be mobilised; for example, one-third would be let go to be replaced by new men. And in 1993, there was also the beginning of compulsory military service, and once they did their compulsory military service, a young man could be mobilised. And now if somebody did not express a wish that they wanted to sign a professional contract, then they were let go, and if they wanted to become professionals, then they would be assigned to barracks, in the same way as, for example, the legionnaires of France or any other professional army that live a soldier's life 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the R brigades, did the men in R brigades have contracts or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they did not have contracts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So I'm understanding much better now. As to those who had contracts, they were supposed, under contract, to be 100 per cent soldiers. Should the Croatian Army tell them to go to a given country, they will go, no question about it, and parents have nothing to say about it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Those brigades had the right to refuse to go anywhere which was contrary to the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia. The Constitution of the Republic of Croatia says not a single soldier of the Croatian Army, regardless of his status, does not have to wage war outside the borders of the Republic of Croatia if they didn't want to do so. Everybody knew that because we said it publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you've already answered my constitutional question I was about to ask you. Did Mr. Tudjman have the sovereign power, his sole power, to decide that a Croatian soldier could fight outside the borders of the republic, and if he decided so, did this decision not have to be ratified by the Sabor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, he could not make a decision that was contrary to the constitution. It goes without saying. Now, whether he could use his authority and issue an order to the Guards Brigade and be obeyed, this is in the realm of speculations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question. If the Serbs attack Croatia and the higher military command in the Croatian Army were to say that a counter-attack has to be launched, possibly in doing so invading the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to catch the Serbs -- to catch -- was that possible or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was possible, Your Honour, and it did happen after Storm in 1995, but that was only after the military agreement was signed between Alija Izetbegovic or, rather, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Franjo Tudjman, when Croatian units had crossed over and liberated one big part of Bosnia and Herzegovina and prevented a slaughter in Bihac, which would have been even worse than in Srebrenica, and they reached Banja Luka. But all that was with the blessing of the United States of America. Unfortunately, we had to seek their approval, and they gave it to us after they had seen what happened in Srebrenica. And then when the Croatian Army, together with the HVO and together with the BiH Army, but still it was the Croatian Army, and when they reached the outskirts of Banja Luka, then the Americans called Franjo Tudjman and said, Stop your troops, you must not advance any further. And since he was a very realistic politician and he knew very well what the powers were on the international political scene, he stopped his troops, and he gave up on this particular military success because of the American ultimatum. America did not issue a similar ultimatum to the Serbs three years previously to stop doing what they were doing. These are the facts, unfortunately that I know so perfectly well, and I am telling you that this is the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One very last question because -- before I give the floor to Judge Trechsel. You were very well informed. You were deputy minister of defence. You took part in Defence Council meetings, and you were an HVO commander. As far as you know in 1992 and 1993, at any point in time did the USA say, Do not attack the ABiH, it is forbidden? Were you made aware of any prohibition coming from the USA or did you [as interpreted] just turn a blind eye and let you do whatever you wanted to do, or were they faced with a fait accompli if there was an attack at all, because I'm always talking conditionally because I have no evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to mention any names. The gentleman has recently testified in the Gotovina case, but I will not say the gentleman's name. He was an American military attache, and he was well informed about everything that was happening in the territory under the control of the HVO in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He went down there, I met with him, and he knew how many volunteers from the Croatian Army were down there. At the request of my Defence team, he provided a statement to this Trial Chamber which will probably be disclosed at the moment when this becomes admissible. In other words, the Americans expressly made us understand that the Croatian Army was not allowed to cross over to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Praljak. I may have to issue a redacting order, because I have to ask you a question. Let's move back into closed session or private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, we are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm really making an effort here. As the state was a young one, I also had a certain task to carry out, so regardless of whether there were professionals or not, the political situation was interpreted. The IPD had to interpret the political situation. People had information about -- so people could have information about what was going on. And here it also says that the latest events in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Muslim offensive in Central Bosnia is referred to, so because of that information of the Muslim attack, there was much interest -- interest had increased in the events, since they were aware of the political situation. So the members of the guards had to know about this, too. Parents are parents, you know. In a normal army, when you have an adult who has signed a professional contract, well, then you can't imagine parents going to ask where their son is. That is why Croatia wasn't at the time such a state. It was just the beginnings. Parents came to ask about the situation. I don't know, but a professional soldier, an adult, signed a contract, and he can't tell his parents, I'm on such and such a battle-field, for God's sake. I was faced with such a problem, if you remember. I don't know whether this was shown here, but on one occasion I spoke to the journalists. So those boys reported home, and then the journalist would say he's greeting his mother from such and such a position. You know, if the enemy was listening to the radio, they'd know exactly where the Croatian troops were deployed. You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You're going astray. Thank you. You have answered my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's complicated. I've gone astray.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, I apologise for having taken some time on these matters, but these were important questions and we needed to address them in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, just to round off this document, then, this topic, let me just put you -- the Prosecution came case to you. You've indicated that President Tudjman actually couldn't legally order HV soldiers to go down and fight in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so the fact is when they write "southern front" in all these documents, that's a way to cover up the fact that HV -- Croatian Army soldiers are being sent down to fight in Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct? It's a cover-up to use the term "southern front," because he couldn't legally do what he was doing; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct, Mr. Stringer, it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's just --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a matter of life and death, about people being wounded. If a volunteer didn't go through the southern front and was killed, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You don't agree that using the term "southern front" was a cover-up to hide the fact that they were being sent down. I put that to you. You deny that, and I think that we can move on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the next document is P03886. This is dated just a few days after the document we just looked at. This is from the 2nd of August, 1993. In fact, at this time -- at this time, General, you've now taken over the command of the Main Staff of the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And do you recognise that this is a document from General Petkovic, directed to the Main Staff of the Croatian Army and General Janko Bobetko?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what's happening here is that General Petkovic is informing General Bobetko, in paragraph 1, he's going to take over responsibility for the Tactical Group 2, and then he gives us the zone of responsibility area, saying that he will occupy it with HVO forces. Then in paragraph 2, he says: "I do not want to use the forces which you shifted to the Tactical Group 2 (HV) in the territory of the HZ-HB without written approval for their use." So first question, General, is: When General Petkovic here is referring to Tactical Group 2, do you know is he referring to a unit of the 5th Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he's not referring to that, and no one in the courtroom knows where the zone of Tactical Group 2 is, and you never drew a map so that we could see where it is. This is your duty when you want to prove something. Tell me, where was Tactical Group 2 located, I mean, really?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not interested not in where they were located, I'm interested in who they were attached to. So you tell me, General, what unit of the Croatian Army, if you know, was Tactical Group 2 attached to? And if you don't know, I'll accept your answer. There's no problem.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know, but it makes no sense to examine me like this. It's harassing the witness, it's a matter of concealing the truth. I would like to see a map of Bosnia-Herzegovina so we could see where Tactical Group 2 is located. What are you doing is an attempt to conceal the truth, and this is something that I won't accept. Where is Tactical Group 2 located, and who was being defended by Tactical Group 2? Where is Popovo Polje and where is Drenovac?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me read paragraph 2 to you: "I do not want to use the forces which you shifted to the Tactical Group 2 (HV) in the territory of the HZ-HB without written approval for their use." Now, on this day, General, you are the commander of the Main Staff of the HVO. I'm asking you: Do you know what is the area which this Tactical Group 2 of the HV was deployed by General Bobetko?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can show you. I can show you where Tactical Group 2 was located. It's not a matter of words; it's a matter of having a look at a military map. If you show me a military map, I will indicate their location for you. You're playing with words, and you're asking me where Tactical Group 2 is. That's below the belt, so I'd like to see a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you confirm for me that the location where the Tactical Group 2 was deployed was within the area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you -- do you agree with what's indicated here, where General Petkovic says that Janko Bobetko shifted the Tactical Group 2 of the Croatian Army in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; do you agree with that? Were you aware of that at the time, you had a Tactical Group 2 that was at least partially present in the area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you show us a map so that I can show you where this occurred, so I can show the territory? It was in the area of incorporation of border-line units. Izetbegovic and Tudjman had signed this agreement. Tactical Group 2 was defending Croatia, the borders of Croatia. You're just speculating here, and you want to lead me to say something that I don't want to say. You want to pretend that I'm ignorant. You're playing with words, and you want to prove something that is not correct. Given the agreement on trans-border cooperation between Alija Izetbegovic and Tudjman, the Croatian Army could be in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the purpose of tactical depth, if you know what that terms me. And if you don't know, I'll explain it to you. And even under such conditions --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, you don't need to question my motives. I'm going to be putting the Prosecution case to you for a number of weeks. I'm trying my utmost to allow you to answer the questions fully, without giving the lengthy answers that you've been allowed to give throughout the course of your testimony. You're not going to have as much leeway with me, if I have anything to do with it. I'm sure you understand that. You've seen a lot of cross-examination throughout the course of this trial, so I think that if we can both try to just focus on the questions and the answers, and focus less on what you think my motives are, I think it will ultimately be more productive. Are you saying that the Tactical Group 2 that's referred to here is a unit that, in your view, was legally present in Bosnia-Herzegovina pursuant to an agreement with President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely legally. I don't have any doubts about your motives, but your logic which you use to confuse matters and to prove your thesis, well, I won't accept this. You can have your motives, but you're showing a general document, so without showing a map, and I don't think this is an honest way of proceeding. But this is your right. Mr. Petkovic says without written authorisation. Written authorisation concerns volunteers. This document is quite clear. The entire document is clear. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'll move on when I'm ready, General, and I'm not quite there yet. The question then is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you must avoid the other party -- from being a party to this exchange. The Prosecutor is doing its job. It so happens that as part of its case, the Prosecution states that the Croatian Army intervened in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and as far as the Prosecutor is concerned, the document establishes this since the Tactical Group 2, which is under the command of the Croatian Army, is in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This document shows General Petkovic tells General Bobetko that he has no intention of using these people unless he is being given a written order or permission to do so. So someone reading this document realises the following: The Tactical Group 2 is in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and General Petkovic is wondering how he can use this. Mr. Stringer says here is a document which, according to him, proves his case. You should then answer his question by explaining what this tactical group was doing there and, as far as you know, why Mr. Petkovic -- why did Mr. Petkovic not intend to use these men if he didn't receive a written order. It's very simple.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, it's not. Here, Petkovic says that the Popovo Polje-Drenovac zone, which is in the south of Croatia and is two kilometres from the Croatian border, in fact, well, the Croatian border is being defended, and Petkovic says that, I'll take that area with HVO forces. He says the Croatian Army should move. That's nonsensical. In military terms, it's nonsensical, because the Croatian Army is defending Croatia here. But the Americans had an objection. It's illogical, it's incomprehensible. So they said, Okay, move them, too. Then Petkovic says, Bring the HVO in and they should move. Although there was this agreement on transporter cooperation between Tudjman and Izetbegovic, which was never annulled, and then it says, The units that you used in the area of Tactical Group 2, forces that I'm returning to you, because I won't use them in the HZ without written authorisation from you, and written authorisation can't be issued by anyone unless they're volunteers. So I cooperate with the Court and I'm asking for the same kind of cooperation, but I'm not someone who will allow others to lead me to tell something that is not the truth. I won't tell you anything that is not the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, the document didn't say this, but you are telling us that this area, Popovo Polje-Drenovac, is on the border with the Republic of Croatia and that the tactical group was in depth two kilometres away from the frontier. General Petkovic realises that and addresses himself to Bobetko and tells him that he doesn't want to use these people unless, of course, he is being given something in writing; was that how the situation stood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you can see in the first item, we first of all had to bring in the HVO. The HV was free, and there was this constant misunderstanding. I quarrelled with the Americans, Why are we defending the border of the Republic of Croatia? We're just defending the border of the Republic of Croatia here, the HV -- the HVO, but there was this Muslim offensive, 700 people went off in one direction, I was mad, I was angry, as a commander, because the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina wasn't being defended there. The Serbs were there from Dubrovnik. Well, that's Popovo Polje. But look, we're searching for the truth. No one wants to show a map, because they're trying to conceal the truth. Otherwise, you should show me a map. I'll draw the situation for you and it will be clear for everyone, but unfortunately we're trying to avoid determining what the truth is here. But I'll repeat this. Bosnia and Herzegovina isn't being defended, but Croatia is. Unfortunately, I used up 700 people, 700 men, and then we managed to liberate some people, and in that territory we quarrelled about who should be involved in defence there, who should defend what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, what you've just said is something you could have said to Mr. Stringer quite calmly, without any problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said everything already, Your Honour. I said it at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next document is P03957, 3957, and do you recognise this as a document that you made?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this document. It was created on the basis of a request of mine. I didn't draft it, I didn't sign it, but I said that this document should be drafted, so it's as if it were my document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well. And this is dated the 4th of August, 1993, so it's a few days after you took command of the Main Staff on the 24th of July, so it's about two weeks after, I think, ten days?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, eight days after I assumed those duties, or let's say two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what you're doing here is issuing a request to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia and to Mr. Susak, personally, requesting that certain officers of the Croatian Army be posted to the Main Staff of the HVO. So I'm assuming or is it correct, General, that you wanted these people to come down and work for you in the Main Staff to help you do your job?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reached an agreement with those individuals, according to which they would assist in the Main Staff as volunteers, and I asked Susak to make them available as volunteers. It says quite explicitly. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We all know that then Brigadier Tole did, in fact, come down and take the position of Chief of Staff of the Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you were actually requesting that Brigadier Kapular come down and take the position of I think it's assistant to the Chief of Staff. I don't know if my translation's got it just right. I have the impression that rather than Kapular coming, what happened is that General Matic came instead. Is that how it ended up? Tole came as Chief of Staff, and then Matic, not Kapular, came and took the position of assistant Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did Kapular come and take a position in the Main Staff of the HVO, as requested here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For combat readiness. I don't know if anyone knows what that means, "combat readiness," the Main Staff, or, rather, I had assistants for combat readiness for the infantry and so on and so forth. Kapular was to assume some of those duties. He did assume certain duties. I don't know when Gojko Susak released him, I couldn't say so right now, but he released him. And he was born in a village near Capljina and he assumed certain duties in the HVO Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, based on what we were talking about yesterday, would it be correct to say that during the time they assumed duties in the HVO Main Staff, that Brigadier Tole and also Brigadier Kapular remained on the payroll of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, did Brigadier Kapular remain as -- despite assuming these duties or his role in the Main Staff for combat readiness, did he at the same time keep his position as commander of the 5th Guards Brigade of the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite certain that at the time he wasn't acting as the commander of the guard, so someone else was replacing him until he returned to the Croatian Army. So the position he previously had was frozen temporarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, is it true, General, that during this period of time, August-September -- July, August, September of 1993, there were, in fact, various components of the 5th Guards Brigade that were deployed and were fighting as part of the HVO in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that some of the members of the 5th Guards Brigade, some of the volunteers, participated in the battle-field as HVO units in Mostar, in Bijelo Polje at the beginning, but mostly in Vakuf, but the figure was never more than 250 men at any given point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit, General, is P04046, 4046, dated 9th of August, 1993. Again, this is the time when you were commander of the HVO Main Staff. This is a document appearing over what appears to be the signature of Milivoj Petkovic. Do you recognise this as a document from General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is General Petkovic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And now he's writing to the minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia, so that would be Mr. Susak, and he makes reference to a meeting in Grude on the 2nd of August, which is one week prior to the date of this document. And I'm asking -- my first question, General, is whether you know or can recall the meeting on the 2nd of August, 1993, that General Petkovic refers to, or whether a meeting took place, because it's with regard to a request for a meeting in Grude, so I'm not -- I'm asking you, the meeting in Grude that's referred to here, do you know if this took place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that the meeting did take place. I don't know whether it was on the 1st or 2nd of August anymore, but I know that the meeting was held. This is when we managed to regain the lost positions in Vakuf. In the evening, after we had taken back these positions, I went to that meeting. I knew everyone present there, and I know the reason for which this meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us, General, who was present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gojko Susak, Mate Boban, Jadranko Prlic, Milivoj Petkovic, Valentin Coric, Siljeg, Bruno Stojic - I'm not 100 per cent certain, but I think Mr. Stojic was also present - and myself, perhaps. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of the meeting was, as far as Boban and Prlic and Petkovic and others were concerned, was the following: On that same morning, they had received information that all -- all to the last defence lines in Gornji Vakuf had fallen the previous night and that the complete population and troops from Gornji Vakuf were on their way towards Rama and further afield. Mr. Susak, on the other hand, had arrived because two days prior to the meeting, 15.000 refugees from Bugojno, and 1.500 troops together with them, crossed the Croatian border. There was some unrest and disorder in Makarska, the situation was desperate, and he simply came to see what the situation was like and what would happen to those men. They all wanted to go to Croatia. All the troops wanted to go to Croatia. They wanted some monies to be paid to them for them to be able to buy something and make a living. The refugees were in a desperate situation, and that was the reason why Susak came. And as for the rest, their reason was the fall of Vakuf, and there was an imminent danger that the entire HVO in Bosnia and Herzegovina would crumble to pieces within five or six days. When I arrived at the meeting that evening, I told them that I had managed to pull my men back. I climbed on a tank, took hold of a machine-gun, and went in the opposite direction, and then I was followed by individual groups and others. And just like in an American movie, in the very war-like military way, I single-handedly managed to restore all the military positions and all the lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 10 to 4.00. It's time for a break, a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, a piece of information. The Registry eventually told us that we, the Prlic Trial Chamber, will sit tomorrow afternoon, not in the morning, which solves the problem raised earlier. So we shall convene in Courtroom I at quarter past 2.00. Ms. Pinter, I think you have something to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Registrar has informed me about the new procedure aimed at correcting the transcript. I would like to say something about yesterday's transcript. The date was 13 July 19 -- 2009. On page 42931, line 13, the text reads: [In English] "It came from the northern side." [Interpretation] This should be replaced by "it came also from the northern side." Furthermore, page 42964, line 9, the original text reads "after," and it should read or should be replaced by "before." Page 42974, line 11, it says "all other situation," and it should say, because that's what was said, "this citation." And as for today's record, page 38, line 14 and line 18, it wasn't "troops" that was said, but "soldiers." "Troops as units," and the witness said "soldiers as soldiers." Thank you, Your Honour. I've been informed that from now on, this is how we should intervene and correct the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. Pinter, I hear that there is a new procedure. Well, I'm very amazed, because I never was told that something had been changed compared to what was done before. Beforehand, what everybody said was transcribed into the English transcript. If there was any uncertainty, everything was corrected after listening to the audio tracks, and the French version was sent to the Trial Chamber the day after or the day following, the next day, and the officer -- the legal officer would check. Now, I have the feeling that an entire factory has been set up, because now the Defence will have to really appeal the transcript, check whether every word has been translated properly, and if there is any approximate translation from B/C/S into English, the same will have to be done from B/C/S into French. I, as the Presiding Judge, listen to what is being said, and if I find that there is something that doesn't quite match, I check the English transcript to see whether there's a problem, but I cannot spend my entire time on watching the transcript. Out of courtesy, I look at the person speaking to me, so here I speak to Mr. Praljak - that's the very least you can do - and if Mr. Stringer speaks, I look at him, and it's up for the legal officer and the Registrar to check the transcript. More often than not, I realise that if there's a problem, it's an interpretation problem. We're not going to spend the entire hearing time on having people on their feet to say, This or that page has to be changed. I don't know who had this great idea of starting a new procedure. This Tribunal's been working for 15 years, and whilst we are just about to close the doors, we discover that the procedure has to be changed. Crazy, it's absolutely crazy. Of course, Defence counsel, accused, who know both languages, whenever they notice something, they point it out, and I thank them for this, I thank them for the work, but this shouldn't be asked of everybody. So everybody does their best. What matters is what is being heard. When Mr. Praljak speaks, I listen to what he says. When I realise that there is something that doesn't quite fit, I put questions to him to make everything clear. So let us proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just to inform you, I spent most of the break trying to persuade Mr. Mundis to join the trial tomorrow. I know that he's been appearing before the President in another case that was suspended, so I thought he'd like to rejoin us for a day. But he resisted my suggestion, so it's good that the Registrar found a different solution. He sends his regards to the Chamber, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, just to stay for one last few moments with Exhibit P04046, we were just talking about this document that was from General Petkovic to Minister Susak, and this relates to advancement/promotion to a rank of the following officers, and it names Stanko Matic there as well as Zarko Tole. Now, I wanted to ask whether these two individuals received a promotion within the Croatian Army, as appears to be reflected in this document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you confirm that at or about this time, the 9th of August, 1993, Mr. Tole became the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then Stanko Matic also held the position of deputy Chief of Staff within the Main Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. He was a general in the JNA, and he was retired before the beginning of the war that we're talking about, and that was his position, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then just consistent with what we've been talking about earlier, would it be correct to say that during the time these two gentlemen served in the Main Staff of the HVO, that they remained on the payroll of the Croatian Ministry of Defence, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot either confirm or deny this. But if you will allow me, what Judge Antonetti asked me about P01332, I looked at the document, I deciphered it, and it says there he's going to be paid in the HVO; P01332, about the group of people, where it says what I was supposed to -- they will be paid by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll check that one. I don't believe I have that one with me.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. The next exhibit, General, is P04061. This is dated the 9th of August, 1993, so it's the same day as the previous document that we were just looking at. And this is a document that appears over the signature of Zarko Tole; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was signed by Matic on behalf of Zarko Tole. I believe this is Matic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so, then, as of the 9th of August, it appears then that Brigadier Tole is, in fact, acting as the Chief of Staff of the HVO Main Staff, and Mr. Matic is acting as his deputy or on his behalf?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were their positions and functions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, this is a report that is directed to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, to the president of the Republic of Croatia, personally, and to the defence minister, personally. General, was it normal or customary, during the time that you were commanding the Main Staff, that reports like this would go to the Croatian Defence Ministry or to individuals such as President Tudjman and Minister Susak?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not customary. Obviously, Brigadier Tole did this of his own will. I didn't do that, and he was not in a position to do that. He was not allowed to do that, but he did. This was not customary, and I suppose that he did it for his own ego. He did not have my leave to do that. I, myself, never drafted such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So would you agree with me, however, that at this period of time, based upon the events that you were talking about just before the break, President Tudjman and Minister Susak would have been extremely interested in the events that were taking place in the territory of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I apologise. They were interested in that. They had to be interested in that. They participated in international negotiations, upon invitations by the international community, and they were duty-bound as a result of an agreement signed with Alija Izetbegovic, and the constitution imposed an obligation on them to look after the Croatian people wherever these people may reside.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the second sentence of the document, so there's a reference again to the Tactical Group 2. I'll just read this: "Tactical Group 2 will be under the command of the southern front. In this respect, the withdrawal of a battalion from the 4th Brigade was made possible for us (364 men). In addition to this battalion, one company each was withdrawn from Grude and Citluk (240 men). "By withdrawing these troops, we have the possibility of strengthening the defence lines at which we are currently located." Now, General, this is a report on the situation at the war front of Herceg-Bosna, especially Gornji Vakuf. My first question is this: The reference to the 240 men, the company -- "one company each was withdrawn from Grude and Citluk (240 men)," were those 240 men members of the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Grude and Citluk are in Herzegovina, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the 364 were -- men were from Ljubuski. In other words, the Ljubuski Brigade consisted of men from Ljubuski, Grude, and Citluk, and those were all HVO troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And are they saying here that those men are being withdrawn and that they're going to be redeployed in the Gornji Vakuf area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. Stringer. I can provide you with a complete explanation. I sent Mr. Tole there, down there, and I said that we would pull out from TG-2 because I was not going to defend the Croatian borders. It was up to the Croatian Army to defend them as best as they could, because I needed my men to stop the all-out Muslim offensive. I did not want to lose the war. The Croatian Army would be best advised to defend the area. If not, I was withdrawing anyway. We were there defending the Croatian borders, which I was not going to do anymore; hence this order. Petkovic came first with his men, and then I said, No, I don't accept that. I will lose a war to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I really don't like being a loser, I don't like losing any wars.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next document, General, is P04194, 4194.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. General Praljak, in this document we have in front of us, which is an important document - nobody will deny that - you say that Zarko Tole sent this report without informing you and that he had a problem of ego. It may be true. We all know about ego problems, so that can happen, indeed. But regardless of that, this document shows that on the southern front, he has received five tanks. On page 2, he's asking for ten tanks to be sent, together with a company for the tanks. So undeniably, logistically speaking, he's asking the Croatian Army to support them. There's a problem with munition, with rocket-launchers, et cetera. As regards the tanks, is it true that you asked the Croatian Army to provide ten tanks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I requested to be provided with a certain number of tanks, if possible. I can't tell you exactly that, but he is requesting assistance here. He says, Please assist us with the following. Second of all, and in the following bullet point he says, If possible from the 5th Guards Brigade, those who want to come to this theatre of war. Your Honours, I did ask assistance from the Croatian Army based on the spirit of voluntarism in order to stop the Muslim offensive. I requested assistance in men, arms, and tools, and here it says that there were 532 troops from the HVO in the theatre of war, they were all volunteers, and this is all -- there were 500 soldiers. There were never any more at any time. They're all volunteers, HV volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Brigadier Tole is seemingly Chief of Staff of the Main Staff, so he's not the number one; you are the number one. So how is it that he can write directly to the president and to the defence minister without going through you first? It is rather amazing, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would have been surprising if the situation was not the way it was. However, on the 9th of August, I was in Gornji Vakuf, fighting for my dear life, fighting for survival. Communications were -- and not only because of communications, but because of 20-hour-long days of waging wars, and that was the situation, I could not control this document. And in that world, there was a desire to communicate directly with Franjo Tudjman, Minister Susak. That made people important. They could then say, I am an important person because I said this and that to Mr. Tudjman. This is one sort of a preliminary or previous psyche, but I don't want to go into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be clear, you said that you were testifying for the truth to be established, and my questions are always within that framework. You can read this document in two ways. One way is that the HVO is in a quandary, in a difficult situation. You conduct the fighting in Gornji Vakuf in August. The situation is extremely difficult, and Mr. Tole, without speaking to you about it, deems it urgent to seek assistance from the Republic of Croatia; hence the document. That's one possible reading of it. Second possible reading of it, as part of the overall control by the Republic of Croatia over the HVO, you and Mr. Tole are on the HV's payroll, since there are personal links between you all, Mr. Tole sends a situation report to the Republic of Croatia, saying, This goes well, this goes wrong, you need to help us. He then addresses those who are -- who have the power of doing something about it, since they can act through the HVO. So there are two possible readings of the document. You are a clever man. You have no doubt understood the purpose of my question. So which is the reading you would recommend of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no doubt about the fact that we did ask for assistance, no doubt at all. Now, why he wrote to the president of a state, it is a bit odd, but nevertheless it's neither here nor there. We did ask for assistance -- I did, at the very outset when I asked for two professional battalions. We did not receive that, we did not receive assistance. We received volunteers, ammunition, a certain number of tools that would accompany the volunteers. We did receive assistance in the form of volunteers. Your Honour Judge Antonetti, that was at the same time when the BH Army, if you will remember, a month before that, the BH Army had set up its logistic bases, the Main Staff of the BH Army; in Zagreb, Split, Sombor and so on and so forth. They collected weapons there. Those weapons were then packed into humanitarian aid, and Petkovic and I let that humanitarian aid go through to Vakuf, and those weapons were turned against us and killed us, and they recruited the same volunteers according to the same principle as this. This is all very complicated. I want to testify. However, this is very complicated. It's so complicated. This is simply how it was. The BiH Army in Croatia, the Main Staff had its own bases, and we let weapons go through, and the same weapons were then used against us to kill us. And then what the Croatian Army was giving us by way of salary, that was from the monies that the citizens of Herzegovina paid into an account. Those were our joint monies. When you omit one part of the truth, you lose the whole truth. It was not Croatia that was in charge of that, because I would not have requested for assistance. I was always imploring, requesting. We had ammunition to wage just one day of war, sometimes that was just the case, and on the other hand at letting through the convoys of the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit is P04194 [Realtime transcript read in error "P1994"]. I've just been telling the Trial Chamber about the assistance that you were requesting from the Republic of Croatia. The fact is, General, you and the HVO received an incredible amount of assistance, military support, soldiers, weaponry, and that weaponry and those soldiers were, in fact, deployed in Bosnia and Herzegovina and to fight against the Armija of Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This document -- well, let's go through this document and then I'll put the question to you again. This is a report from a Captain Alen Klopopan. He's with the 7th Guards Brigade. It's dated the 15th of August, 1993, and the subject is: "Report on combat operations in the HZ-HB."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, there is a mistake in the transcript. It's not P1994, but P04194.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you. P04194.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In this report, General, the captain is reporting that at 1745 hours on the 13th of July, 1993, he was ordered to send two armoured personnel carriers, APCs, and two crews to conduct a combat mission in Herceg-Bosna, and then he goes on to describe what happened to these two APCs; they first went to Tomislavgrad, crews reported to General Glasnovic there, they went to Ramsko lake, they were attached to the Zrinski special unit and Colonel Filipovic. Then on the 19th of July, the APCs then were taken down to Gornji Vakuf where they participated in combat operations over the next few days. And skipping down toward the end of that paragraph, on the 31st of July the most important parts of the weapons and electronic systems were removed. This is because the APCs had been severely damaged, I believe. "Since there was very little time and an order was received to withdraw, the APC had to be destroyed. The men returned to our unit on 1 August 1993." Now, General, you've been talking about the severity of the conflict that was taking place in the Gornji Vakuf area at this period of time in August, and in fact you were present in the Gornji Vakuf area during these conflicts in August; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there when the APCs were destroyed. I was in close proximity, I was next to them. I am aware of the incident. You're talking about BOVs which had arrived there and they're from that same brigade at my request. Unfortunately, only a few days later the BiH Army destroyed both of them because they hit an anti-tank mine. Fortunately enough, the crews went unscathed and they returned on the 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that there was fierce fighting going on because the BiH Army was well equipped with the weapons that was arriving from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And despite your assertions about volunteers, what's written -- and this report indicates, in fact, that the APC crews that were sent down there were sent on orders, that they were not volunteers; they were in fact ordered to go down there and to participate in these combat operations in Herceg-Bosna; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not correct. I've already explained, and if you want me to do so, I'll repeat. First, the volunteers decided to be volunteers, and then the order was issued in order to regulate their social and other rights in case there were dead and wounded, because subsequently when their families had to deal with their pension, they had to evoke a document, and if they were called volunteers, they would not have been entitled to anything. The red tape is most [indiscernible]. Bureaucrats would say, You're a volunteer, you went to a different state, you're entitled to nothing. First I told them they would go down there as volunteers, and then I said, Okay, now issue an order so that my family can eat and that I can be treated in a hospital in case I am wounded. That's how things went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I believe you haven't understood Mr. Stringer's question. You have told us that the volunteers needed documents in case they died, in case they were wounded. That I understand perfectly, but this is not what the issue hinges on. You have a document before you that indicates that two armoured vehicles, which were clearly attached to the Zrinski unit, took part in the fighting. We don't know who the crew is because the names do not figure on this document, but we have every reason to believe that these people are not volunteers because they received an order to go there and they go. The Prosecutor is telling you, General Praljak, we have a document before us that establishes that the Croatian Army is present on the battle-field. This what the problem is all about. We have a document that shows that two armoured vehicles are destroyed, that the crew comes from Croatia, and then they go back to Croatia. What explanation do you have for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My explanation is the same. I asked Filipovic, Colonel Filipovic, who was in charge of a unit, who was a member before this war of the French Foreign Legion, I asked him if he could come and provide me with assistance. He came with perhaps 20 men, and then I told him, because this position referred to here, Is it possible to bring two APCs so that we can try to stop them here? And then there was this search. And when Filipovic, Kapular, and these crews were found, well, then a request was drafted. Then this man received a request, and he says, I received a request. But, Judge Antonetti, before that request, as in the case of some members of the 1st Guards Brigade, the 40th one, before I phoned, because I knew certain commanders, I asked whether they could come as volunteers to assist. And when they said, Yes, well, then an order is written, and only for the reasons that I have mentioned. So this isn't an order. If an order were drafted in this way, then two of them wouldn't have arrived, ten tanks would have arrived, 20 APCs, helicopters, we would have included three guards brigades, and we would have routed the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, but you have been asked actually the same question first by Mr. Stringer and afterwards by Judge Antonetti. It is again you are, in a way, not answering the questions, but you are pleading, and it is very clear in that order, what he says, kind of report, that he was ordered to send two armoured personnel carriers and two crews to conduct a combat mission in Herceg-Bosna. Could you show to me any word here which speaks about volunteers? It is the question, and not something else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm telling you that they are volunteers, that what it says here has to do with the request, the nature of which I have explained to you. I have given you an explanation. I said that an order could be issued to brigades. If it was possible to issue an order to brigades of the Croatian Army, then there wouldn't have been 500 men, as it says in the document down there. Three Croatian brigades would have been sent down there, and the war would have been quite different. But there is a word that I have explained. If you want to interpret this to say that an order could have been issued, well, I'm telling you that's not the case. It says "order." Well, people weren't really taking account of this to say it's an order on the basis of volunteers having reported.
